study.title: Psalm 29 The voice of the LORD on creation and his people
study.overview: This psalm is a hymn of exaltation to the LORD, presented as the one worthy of absolute honor. The text begins by calling the mighty to recognize the glory of God and ends by showing that the same God who rules the storm also strengthens and blesses his people with peace. The dominant image is that of the "voice of the Lord," which shakes, breaks, raises and dominates everything, suggesting that no force of nature, and no human power, competes with him. At the same time, the psalm does not end in fear, but in confidence: the eternal King gives strength to his people and blesses him with peace.

outline.title: Invitation to the worship of the mighty
outline.explanation: The initial verses call the "sons of the mighty" to attribute to the LORD glory, strength, and honor due to his name. Worship must be reverent, holy and conscious of the divine majesty.

outline.title: The voice of the LORD dominates the storm
outline.explanation: The repetition of "the voice of the Lord" describes a powerful and majestic manifestation of God in nature. The thunder, the breakup of the cedars and the tremor of creation communicate strength, sovereignty and reverent fear.

outline.title: God reigns forever and blesses his people
outline.explanation: The rest of the psalm widens the effects of this voice on fire, desert, animals and forest, until they declare that in the temple all speak of the glory of God. The climax is that the Lord reigns forever and gives his people strength and peace.

study.context: The notes suggest that the psalm was composed in connection with a strong storm, with thunderstorm, lightning and rain. This reading helps to understand why the text repeatedly speaks of God's "voice" as something audible and tremendous. It is also mentioned that the psalmist calls the mighty to recognize the supremacy of the LORD, contrasting any human pretense of power with divine authority over creation.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that creation is not autonomous: it answers the word and voice of the LORD. The same God whose voice frightens and destabilizes nature is the God who establishes his eternal reign and takes care of his people. There is here a theology of divine sovereignty: it governs seas, forests, deserts and even the most impressive forces of the earth. At the same time, this sovereignty is neither cold nor distant. The King who reigns over everything also gives strength to his people and blesses him with peace. In evangelical language, the text invites to reverence, trust and worship: God is fearful in majesty, but kind in his dealings with his own.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm calls the "the heavenly beings" or those who thought of other powers to recognize the Lord as the only God worthy of honor.
The psalmist would have taken the occasion of a great storm to attribute glory to God, interpreting thunder as a call to worship.
The "voice" of the Lord is understood as thunder, an expression of the divine majesty in the storm.

questions: In what ways do I treat God as worthy of practical honor, and not just verbal admiration?
When I see the strength of creation or I face scary situations, does this lead me to fear of God or self-reliance?
How can I seek the peace that God promises without separating it from his sovereignty and holiness?
study.practice: Take aside time to worship God with reverence, recognizing his sovereignty over the world and over his own life. If you are facing fear, instability, or pressure, pray on the basis of verse 11: ask the LORD for strength to obey and peace to rest in it. It is also worth practicing public and private worship with awareness of holiness, avoiding treating God in a casual way.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are truncated in some excerpts, especially in part of Matthew Henry's comment, so not all the details of this reading could be fully confirmed. The context of a storm is a plausible interpretation of the notes, but it cannot be treated as absolute historical certainty. There is also no specific and developed commentary on verse 10, so its function in the flow of the psalm was inferred from the biblical text and the general theme of God's reign.
